My dearest Marie,

The evening light here is peculiar, catching the Rhine in a way that makes one forget the hours. I spent the day among the great two-masted vessels, their sails furled against the quiet water, and wandered through the churches. The stone here holds a weight that speaks of centuries, not just the present moment.

I am to attend the cathedral mass tomorrow morning. The music, I am told, is worthy of the occasion. I shall be accompanied by the young Counts Stolberg and their tutor, Dean Kellermann. We must depart for Aachen this afternoon, so the day is already moving us forward.

Think of me as I stand here, watching the river flow toward the sea. It is a fine, if tired, traveler’s view. Give my regards to the boys. I hope the snuff I purchased in Bonn suits your father.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The Rhine here is grand, heavy with large two-masted vessels that seem to carry the weight of the world. I have spent the day wandering the churches, finding the stone quiet compared to the noise of the streets.

I look forward to the cathedral tomorrow morning. The Counts Stolberg and Dean Kellermann are joining me for the mass; the music is said to be exquisite, a necessary counterpoint to the practicality of our daily lives. It is good to be among those who still value the sacred in art.

I must ride for Aachen this afternoon. The journey is not long, but the roads are dusty. Do not worry for me; I am well and my spirits are high. Keep the house in order and tell the boys I expect them to be diligent in their studies, for freedom is earned through discipline, not given as a gift.

Give my love to the children.

Your faithful,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The evening light on the Rhine is quite something. The river is thick with large two-masted vessels, moving with a purpose that reminds one of the state’s own machinery. I have spent the day wandering the churches, admiring the stone. It is impressive, though one must look past the mere material to see the spirit it houses.

For Sunday, I intend to attend Mass in the cathedral with the young Counts Stolberg and their tutor, Dean Kellermann. The music is said to be excellent. I must be careful, however, not to let the aesthetic subsume the ethical. We are here to observe the religious life of the people, not merely to be entertained.

I hope the boys are well-behaved and that you are finding the Berlin air agreeable. I shall leave for Aachen this afternoon. Pray for my safe passage.

Yours,
G.W.F.

This is my day's work, — of course, I have also seen the Rhine, the endless row of large two-masted ships on it, and a few more churches. Tomorrow morning, Sunday — probably in the company of the young Counts of Stolberg and Dean Kellermann, their teacher for many years, who was present at Stolberg's death — I will still see the cathedral with a musical mass and other things, and then depart for Aachen tomorrow afternoon.

My dearest Marie,

I am settled here in Amsterdam, having arrived shortly after noon. I went straight to Dr. Besseling’s, where Mr. van Ghert’s recommendation opened the door. It is a house of order, which I appreciate after the chaos of travel.

I spent the afternoon in the picture gallery. I confess I was struck dumb before a Rembrandt—fifteen to twenty feet across, twelve high. It is not mere decoration; it is the spirit of the age made visible, the individual soul expanded into the universal. I did not finish the collection, but I have seen enough to know that art here speaks the language of freedom we have only begun to articulate in our own land.

The light in the evening is distinct, grey and clear. I miss the warmth of your hearth and the noise of the boys. Write soon.

Your G. W. F.

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Amsterdam just past noon and went straight to Dr. Besseling, who received me with the warmth Mr. van Ghert had promised. The city is bright, the water everywhere, and the air is sharp.

Afterward, I visited the picture gallery. It is a vast undertaking, but I could not finish the collection today. I spent hours before the Rembrandts. One canvas, fifteen to twenty feet across and twelve high, commands the room with a gravity that stops the breath. It is not mere decoration; it holds a whole world’s suffering and dignity in its strokes. One sees the spirit of the age not in its politics, but in how it renders the human face.

I am tired but content. The journey is good for the mind. I hope the boys are well and that you are keeping your health. I think of you constantly in these quiet evenings.

Your loving,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

I reached Amsterdam shortly after noon, my legs still aching from the journey. I went straight to Dr. Besseling, who received me with the courtesy Mr. van Ghert promised. We spoke little of philosophy, mostly of the weather, which here is as grey as a Nuremberg winter.

Then I visited the picture gallery. The scale of it is staggering; the Rembrandts are vast, fifteen to twenty feet across. Standing before them, one feels the weight of history pressing in. I confess I could not view the whole collection today; the mind requires rest as much as the body.

I hope the boys are well and that you are not too tired. I think of our quiet evenings in Berlin, and how the noise of travel makes one appreciate the silence of home. I will send word when I leave.

Your devoted,
G.W.F.

Arrived here in Amsterdam at 12:07 o'clock, immediately went to Dr. Besseling, to whom I had been recommended by Mr. van Ghert — a very obliging man — then to the painting gallery, — here are works by Rembrandt, 15 to 20 feet wide, 12 feet high, I have not yet seen everything.

My dearest Marie,

The wine in Giessen was excellent, and the company of my colleagues there most lively. We argued over the finer points of logic until the candles burned low, and I must confess I enjoyed the vigorous debate. It is a pleasure to see the spirit of inquiry still alive in these universities.

We have left the main party and are now travelling along the Lahn with a schoolteacher, a man of considerable learning. We passed Weilburg this afternoon; the old princely residence stands quiet against the river, a reminder that power, like thought, must be grounded in its own history to endure. The air is crisp, and the pace is gentle. I am well rested and in good spirits. Do not worry for me; the journey is less a burden than a change of air. I look forward to returning to our study in Berlin to continue our work.

Your devoted husband,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The Lahn runs quiet under the evening sky. We have left the bustle of Giessen, where the professors’ hospitality was warm, though the wine perhaps a touch too generous for an evening walk. I parted ways with our Frankfurt-bound friends, glad to continue with Herr, the schoolteacher. He is a man of quiet intellect, and our conversation along the river bank was pleasant, if not entirely without the friction of differing views on the nature of the state.

We passed Weilburg, that old princely residence, standing silent against the hill. It strikes me as a monument to a time when freedom was the privilege of a few, rather than the substance of all. It is good to see the past recede behind us. I am tired, but my spirits are high. The journey is less about the destination and more about the movement itself. Keep the house warm. I shall write again from Frankfurt.

Your devoted,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

We arrived in Giessen this morning. The professors here are charming, and the wine excellent. I spent the afternoon in lively debate with the theologians, which was most invigorating. We are now traveling down the Lahn with a young schoolteacher. The river is calm, the air fresh.

I passed Weilburg this evening. It is a fine, quiet place, formerly a princely residence. I find myself thinking of our home in Berlin. The distance feels greater when one is moving. I hope the children are well and that Karl is applying himself to his studies. I shall be back before the month is out, I trust.

Do not worry about me. The journey is pleasant. I have enough snuff and my books are secure.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

Then we went to Giessen, a pleasant city and surroundings, with two nice castles in the neighborhood. Here I was with three confreres: the Giessen professor of philosophy—Snell?—the Marburg professor of the same, Creuzer?, a cousin of the Heidelberg one—and an extraordinary professor of theology, a man of striving, insight, and cultivation. But how insipid those my nearer confreres had been, I had to overlook, as the Giessen one immediately led us to wine and treated us with very good vintage. In Giessen was the parting point for those who went to Frankfurt, among whom, as we had agreed at the start, I was not, all the less as I would otherwise have spent longer in the company up to now. My young teaching colleague, the Israelite, however, stuck with me; we followed the Lahn. Weilburg has a romantic location, a beautiful, vegetation-rich, narrow valley, pleasant bends of the Lahn—and also, as a former princely residence, nice houses.

My dearest Marie,

I have reached Kassel, arriving just after eleven. The morning was warm, so I spent it wandering the streets and the gardens, letting my thoughts settle after the journey. The town is pleasant enough, though it lacks the bustle of Berlin. I sat in a quiet corner of the Hofgarten for some time, watching the light change, and found myself reflecting on the peculiar stillness of provincial life here. It is a sharp contrast to the intellectual ferment we know at home.

I hope the boys are well-behaved and that your health is steady. I miss our evenings and the comfort of our library. I shall try to rest well tonight, for we must continue our route tomorrow. Do not worry; the roads are good, and I am in high spirits. Give my love to Karl and Immanuel, and tell them their father is thinking of them as he watches the stars come out over the palace.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Kassel just after eleven. The heat was oppressive, so I spent the day walking the town rather than seeking rest. The air here is thick, but the light is bright and clear. I have taken a room near the castle; the view is pleasant, and the service adequate.

I am tired, but the change of scene does good. I find myself thinking less of the dense abstractions of the *Philosophy of Right* and more of the simple, living world. It is a necessary counterweight. I have bought a small bottle of local wine and a packet of snuff. I shall dine simply and sleep early.

Do not worry for me. The journey is steady. I hope Karl and Immanuel are well and that the heat in Berlin is not too severe for you. I shall write again from Hanover, insha’Allah.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

I am writing from Kassel, where I arrived this morning at eleven. The town is pleasant, though the air is thick with the dampness of the Rhine valley. I spent the entire afternoon walking the streets, observing the architecture and the faces of the people. There is a quiet dignity here, distinct from the bustle of Berlin. I walked until my feet ached, enjoying the solitude and the change of scenery.

I have dined well, though the wine was not quite up to the standard of our home cellar. I am tired but content. The journey continues, but for now, I rest. I think often of you and the boys. Please give my regards to Karl and Immanuel when you next see them. I hope this letter finds you in good health and high spirits.

Yours always,
G. W. F. Hegel

I also arrived in Cassel happily this morning at 11 o'clock, and after having walked about a great deal both in the morning and afternoon, I intend to spend this evening with you, my dear, and with the account of my life and travels up to now.... My journey is not progressing as quickly as I initially intended. It has gone reasonably well for me so far, and for people who have money and stick to the main road, the world is in good condition; — however, it also requires that they have good news from your family; I have departed reassured regarding you; but I cannot be entirely free of worry, and in any case I set out on the road with great reluctance, and I am really only traveling on because I am already on the journey and am supposed to be.

My dearest Marie,

We arrived in Koblenz this evening, the heat finally broken by the river. The journey from Kassel was an exercise in endurance. I was forced to sit facing backward, opposite a Göttingen student who clung to the rear seat with a tenacity that bordered on the absurd. The other passengers were a motley crew; one Englishman abandoned us at the last moment, leaving us with the full weight of six souls in a cramped interior.

I confess I found the backward view of the Lahn’s banks strangely comforting, a constant reminder that progress often requires looking at what has just passed. The river followed the coach faithfully, a mirror to our own restless movement. I am tired, but the wine here is good. I think of you and the boys in Berlin, where the air is still. Do not worry; I am merely traversing, not arriving.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I write from Koblenz, weary but safe. The journey from Kassel was a comedy of discomfort. Six souls crammed into the coach, three to a seat, with the river Lahn rushing past our windows. I sat facing backward, as is my custom, directly opposite a Göttingen student who clung to the rear seat marked number one with a tenacity that bordered on the pathological. He seemed less a traveler than a fixture of the carriage.

We followed the Lahn, the water mirroring the grey sky, while I tried to read a newspaper over the rattle of the wheels. The Englishman who accompanied me to Kassel stayed behind, leaving me to the mercies of the driver and the heat. I am glad to be stationary again. The air here is cool, and I have ordered a bottle of wine to soothe my nerves and my back.

I think of you and the boys. The house feels distant, yet the thought of returning to our calm is my greatest comfort.

Your loving
Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Koblenz today, weary but in good spirits. The journey from Kassel was a study in discomfort. I sat facing backward, which gave me a peculiar view of the Lahn winding behind us, while a young student from Göttingen clung to the seat behind me with the tenacity of a barnacle. We were six souls packed into that box, sweating through our coats.

I find myself thinking of our quiet evenings in Berlin. There is a strange freedom in being alone on the road, yet I miss your voice and the simple order of our home. The Rhine here is magnificent, though the heat is oppressive. I have taken a room above the river. I hope the boys are behaving themselves and that you are not too tired from the household duties. I shall write again tomorrow.

Yours ever,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

I am writing from Cologne, tired but content. The journey has been a mix of rain and reflection. In Koblenz, I waited out the absence of Councillor Lange, which gave me time to sit with my thoughts. Yesterday, I took the boat to Neuwied to visit the Moravian Sisters. Their quiet devotion is striking; one sees the ethical life in its simplest, most earnest form.

This morning, the rain was heavy as I boarded the Rhine steamer. I stopped at Linz to view a painting in a hilltop church, as Schulze advised. It was worth the climb. In Bonn, I called on Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther. We spoke, and the wine was good.

I think of you and the boys here in Berlin. The river moves on, and so do I, but my heart remains with you. Do not worry about my health; the change of air is doing me good. I shall write again soon.

Your loving,
G. W. F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I write from Cologne, though my feet have been in Koblenz and Bonn. The weather turned foul, forcing me into a boat rather than a carriage. I visited the Moravian Sisters in Neuwied; their quiet discipline struck me as a small, orderly world, very different from our chaotic streets. In Bonn, I called on Windischmann and his son-in-law, Walther. The conversation was lively, as usual, though I confess I was tired by the journey. I stopped at Linz to see a painting Schulze had raved about; it was decent, but I would rather have had a glass of wine and a quiet room.

I am well, if somewhat damp. The Rhine is wide and grey tonight. I think of you and the boys in Berlin. Please do not worry about my health; I am merely a bit weary. I look forward to returning to my study and my whist partners.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The journey has been a mixture of damp and discovery. I spent a day in Koblenz, waiting for Councillor Lange who never showed, which left me with nothing but my thoughts and the rain. On Wednesday I took a boat to Neuwied and visited the Moravian Sisters’ House; there is a quiet dignity in their order that one rarely finds these days.

The river has been unkind, and I am soaked through from the journey to Linz. I stopped there to see a painting Schulze mentioned in a hilltop church. It is competent, though not profound. At Bonn, I called on Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther. We discussed the state of affairs in the Rhineland, and I found the men eager, if somewhat confused about their own position in history.

I am tired, but the wine here is excellent. I miss your company and the calm of our home. Do not worry for me; I am merely wet, not ill.

Your affectionate
Georg

So I would have been happy to have arrived in the venerable Imperial City of Cologne.... In Coblenz, where my last letter ends, I spent the afternoon and the following morning mostly resting at home — the Consistory Councillor Lange, to whom Schulze had addressed me, was not present, — and in indecision about the weather I let the express coaches, steam packets, and other opportunities pass by; but on Wednesday afternoon it cleared up; I took a boat and went to Neuwied on the beautiful Rhine; I saw the Moravian Brethren' house; — it became too dark to go into the Prince's Brazilian collection. The most beautiful thing was the evening — beautiful moonlight shone over the Rhine, which flowed past my windows; owls, which I had never heard speak in my life, made music in it, — in the morning after 8 o'clock onto the steam packet, an improved market boat. — At first one could be somewhat on the deck, but then it became windy, cold, rainy, finally continuous, heavy, cold rain. The company was thus confined in the cabin, and there were also students in it, who were making their Rhine journey, so with the knapsack, covered with green oilcloth and with a boot sticking out on each side of it, wide new straps, — everything in order, also white, or rather yellow straw hats. So I, although with somewhat more ballast than they, also made my Rhine journey, but therefore saw less, and was inferior to them in that I could not gain the proud consciousness of making a Rhine journey. Already the rainy weather in Coblenz, — above all this Rhine journeying, had spoiled my travel, and if it had not been so far home to you, above all if I had not been afraid of the post coaches, I would have quickly arrived at your place. I travel in general only out of duty and obligation, and would have a hundred times more satisfaction and pleasure if I could divide my time between my studies and you. If you ever come with me to this Rhine, I will lead you differently; on the water one sees neither the Rhine nor the country, — the former not, for one does not see it flowing through the fields and hills, one does not have it as a part of the picture before one, which is its truly beautiful position or flow — nor the country, for one sees only the banks, their boundaries and notices at most that it might be beautiful behind them. — In Linz we went ashore, where I saw the picture recommended by my friend Privy Councillor Schulze, and that in a high-situated church, from where one overlooks the Rhine and the beautiful country. — In abominable rain we went ashore in Bonn. Here I looked for Windischmann and his son-in-law Walther), whom you know from Thibaut, — with the former, who through union in prayer with Prince Hohenlohe?) has been healed for a year of a six-year eye ailment of the kind like Jacobi's, only much worse — and is now perfectly healthy, I got along very well, and we, for the time being, were very satisfied with each other. Walther also pleased me, who remembers you with very heartfelt remembrance, and sends you friendly greetings. — This encounter refreshed me again. To this was added the clearing up of the weather, and so I set out yesterday afternoon in a better disposition.... Bonn is hawkerish, very narrow-streeted, but the surroundings, view, botanical garden — beautiful, very beautiful, but I am still rather in Berlin.

My dearest Marie,

The light in The Hague is fading as I write. I take the coach to Breda tonight, though I confess the journey seems less a necessity than a whim for fresh air. The Dutch spirit is orderly, but I find myself craving the warmth of our home and the sound of the children’s voices.

I must tell you of a strange sight I passed today. A tomb monument, they say by Michelangelo. Alabaster figures of a count and his wife lie upon a black slab, yet above them stand four giants—Caesar, Hannibal, Regulus—holding up the stone. It struck me as a terrible image of history: the dead held aloft by the weight of past empires, while the living are reduced to mere stone. It made me think of how our own freedom is not a gift from nature, but a struggle carried on by the spirits of ages.

I miss you terribly. The wind is rising, and I feel the need for your steadying presence.

Your devoted,
G.

My dearest Marie,

The evening air in The Hague is crisp, and I am already on the coach for Breda. I write to tell you of a curiosity I saw there: a tomb monument ascribed to Michelangelo. It is a striking piece, showing a count and his wife in white alabaster lying upon a black slab. Above them, four standing figures—Julius Caesar, Hannibal, and Regulus among them—support a second slab at the corners. It is a composition of great dignity, the dead held aloft by the weight of historical virtue. One cannot help but reflect on how the particular lives of these individuals are preserved within the universal structure of the state and history. The alabaster seems to glow against the dark stone, a quiet testament to the permanence of ethical life. I hope the boys are well and that your health holds steady. The journey continues, and I shall write again from the next post.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The heat in The Hague is finally breaking, and I have taken the coach to Breda. I must confess, the journey was tedious, but the city holds a curiosity that arrested me. In the church, I viewed a tomb ascribed to Michelangelo. It is a strange, heavy composition: a count and his wife in alabaster rest upon a black slab, while four standing figures—Julius Caesar, Hannibal, and Regulus, among them—support a second slab above them.

It struck me as a perfect image of the ethical substance. The private individual, the "I," is merely the foundation. It is only when supported by the great, universal forces of history and state that the life gains any true weight or permanence. Without those pillars, the individual is merely a stone in the dust. I think of you and the boys, holding the family together with such quiet strength. I am tired, but my mind is clear. I hope the news from the university is good.

Yours,
G.W.F.

That evening, after I had written to you, I took the carriage to Breda, where I saw the magnificent work by Michelangelo—a mausoleum. Six life-sized figures of white alabaster: a count and his wife, lying in death, and four figures: Julius Caesar, Hannibal, Regulus, and a warrior standing bent over at the four corners of the black stone on which they lie, carrying on their shoulders a similar black stone—a magnificent, spirited work by the greatest master.

My dearest Marie,

The day has been a strange mix of history and hygiene. Here in Aachen, the sexton actually let me sit in Charlemagne’s own coronation chair. It was a curious sensation; one feels the weight of the state not as an abstraction, but as a physical seat. I spent the whole day with Bettendorf, examining his paintings until the light failed, and then walked out to Burtscheid for a sulphur bath. It is a strange remedy, but the water is hot and the air is sharp.

I have since traveled to Liège, arriving late this evening. I am staying with a fellow passenger for the night. The journey is uneventful, but the mind is full. I miss the quiet of Berlin and your company. I shall continue north tomorrow. Give my love to the boys.

Yours,
G. W. F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The Rhine is broad tonight, and the air in Cologne is thick with the scent of the evening. I write from the inn, weary but content.

In Aachen, I spent hours in the cathedral, sitting in the very chair where Charlemagne was crowned. There is a weight to such history that no book can convey. I also spent a long day viewing Bettendorf’s paintings, the man himself present, discussing the works with great passion. It was a good use of time, though I confess my legs ached by the end of the afternoon.

I took a sulphur bath in Burtscheid, which did wonders for my joints. Now I am in Liège, arriving late with a fellow passenger. The journey is tiring, but the spirit is lifted by these encounters with the past.

I think of you and the boys in Berlin. Keep warm.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

I am in Cologne, tired but content. The journey has been pleasant, though my knees protest the sulphur bath I took in Aachen after a long day. I confess I spent hours in the morning and afternoon viewing Bettendorf’s paintings, accompanied by the collector himself. It was a fine display, though I found myself thinking of how art reveals the spirit’s inwardness better than dry philosophy.

The strangest moment came when the sexton let me sit in Charlemagne’s coronation chair. I felt a sudden, absurd weight of history. One imagines the pomp of that era, yet here I sat, just an old professor in a dusty room. It reminded me that even the greatest moments are fleeting, like the smoke from my snuffbox.

I reached Liège late yesterday and stayed with a fellow passenger. The roads are good. I hope you and the boys are well. I think of you constantly.

Yours,
G.W.F.

But they were covered with gold leaf, which had engraved stories on it, of which some pieces are still preserved. On this throne, 300 years after his death, Karl was found sitting, I believe, by Emperor Friedrich, with the imperial regalia put on him, the crown on his head, the scepter in one hand, and the orb in the other; these items were added to the Imperial Regalia and his bones were interred. I sat on this throne, on which 32 emperors had been crowned, as the sacristan assured me, just as well as anyone else, and the whole satisfaction is that one has sat on it. — But the main thing was that I saw the collection of Mr. Bettendorf (which is now being sold individually) for 3 hours in the morning and likewise in the afternoon, and he had the kindness to keep me company himself. In regard to Old German art, it is the counterpart to the Boisseree collection; both combined, as both gentlemen intended — purchased by the King — would represent the most magnificent thing in this sphere of art. Mr. Bettendorf does not have such large and distinguished van Eycks as Boisseree, but his Hemlings, one picture in particular, are at least as excellent as the Boisseree ones. Some of the figures in the Boisseree Hemlings, especially the Jew gathering manna, is exactly the same one who cuts the Paschal lamb on the Bettendorf picture. — But one picture by a Roger is the highest thing one can see; every particularity — some dryness that one would wish to remove even from the most excellent Eyck works — has completely disappeared here; it is as magnificently Italian as it is Netherlandish. A jewel is likewise a picture — a Deposition from the Cross with many figures, drawn by Raphael and painted by Albrecht Dürer, what loveliness, what beauty!! — A woman with a child — attributed by some to Michelangelo — is an infinitely great painting. But above all, a night by Correggio! — just as I called the Dresden one the day of Correggio, so this is the true night. What a picture! The light emanating equally from the child — Mary is dearer to me here than in the Dresden one, and she, like the surroundings in this one, smiles — everything is also cheerful — but more serious, and the darkness, as in the Correggio pictures in Sanssouci, of the later manner of this master — of the highest excellence. In the evening I still took a walk towards Burtscheid, and since the famous bath is in Aachen, I took a bath: it is hot! and full of sulphur smell. — On Tuesday morning at 7 o'clock we left Aachen and arrived in Liège around 5 o'clock; the road goes up hill, down hill, mostly on a ridge, with deeper valleys on both sides, everything green, intersected by innumerable hedges and rows of trees. Towards Liège one gets views into the beautiful Meuse valley; I was very tempted to travel from Liège up the Meuse valley via Namur to here — but I would have spent nearly two days longer, because of the curse of the carriages, and part of the journey would have been made at night, when no one sees anything. In Liège I stayed overnight with one of the travelers; the carriage on which we had arrived went straight on; among the traveling party there was just again such a flat, chatty German — a Würzburger, who also wants to be an Englishman — annoying people, as I had had one in every carriage party so far.
