My dearest Marie,

Vienna is magnificent, even in the rain. The Emperor’s name day was marked by a full house at the Italian Opera. We sat through twenty-nine singers—Fodor, Rubini, among them—shouting the anthem in unison. It was a spectacle of noise rather than subtlety. The rain prevented the usual illuminations, so we missed the visual display, but the German premiere of Auber’s opera was a pleasant surprise. The crowd was spirited, if a bit loud.

I have already sent my luggage off ahead of me. I feel light, ready to move on. Do not worry about the small things here; I am well. I miss your quiet presence in Berlin, but this travel has a certain invigorating quality. I hope the boys are well-behaved and that your health is sound. I shall write again soon from Prague.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

Vienna tonight was a spectacle. The Emperor’s name day brought the whole city to the Italian Opera. I sat amidst the full house, listening to twenty-nine singers—including Rubini and Lablache—strike the anthem in perfect unison. It is a striking display of disciplined harmony, a collective will sublimated into art.

The rain kept the streets dark, sparing us the usual illuminations, which suited my preference for the interior over the exterior. We also saw a German cast premiere an Auber opera. The music was pleasant, but the Italian voices hold a certain natural grace that the German ones, however skilled, lack.

I am well, though my luggage has already departed, leaving me lighter for the journey. I think of you and the boys. The world moves, but my heart remains in Berlin.

Your devoted
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The rain has kept the streets of Vienna dark, sparing us the usual glare of illuminations for the Emperor’s name day. I sat in the Italian opera house, packed tight with the city’s elite. It was a spectacle of voices rather than lights. Twenty-nine singers, including Fodor and Rubini, united in a single chord for the anthem. I confess the sheer volume was dizzying, but there is a certain grandeur in such collective force, even if the music itself is merely pleasant.

Later, a German cast premiered an Auber opera. It was lighter, perhaps more intelligible to the local ear, but lacks the dramatic weight of the Italian tradition. I am weary from the journey and the noise. My thoughts turn to our quiet rooms in Berlin, to Karl and Immanuel, and to the peace of our library. I hope the change of air agrees with you. I shall write again soon.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

Still Vienna! My effects have already been handed over to the shipping agent, — some additions, — the subtractions belong to the travel expenses; — these, however, are no heathen money, but everything was spent on Christians and used for me — also a good Christian. Now, after the completion of such business, to — where? To the Italian Theatre! To — first, the popular song — as today on St. Francis’s Day. — The rainy weather, however, did not allow illuminations to appear, which otherwise would have been perhaps the only celebration of this day; I could learn nothing of any further fuss. I also celebrated this day by listening to the aforementioned song, performed on one side by Mrs. Fodor à la tête, then Dardanelli and so on, 13 in number, and on the other side by Signor David à la tête, Donzelli, also Rubini, Lablache, Ambrogi, Bassi, da Franco etc., 16 men high — although unison, but without solos, variations. So for such means not enough action, — the men in black, the ladies in white satin! The house was this time packed full, probably for Francis’s Day, also for the sake of the German Opera, which was given for the first time today, — French music performed by Germans and German women. On the one hand, because of the packed full house, I had for the first time the opportunity to see very many, i.e., several pretty ladies, and on the other hand I could notice more of the Viennese ladies on my part, because I did not have to see and hear Italians and Italian women on the stage. I also pass from that to the German Opera, i.e., the French charming music by Auber, performed by German throats! In the last act, passion comes into the voices through a French coup, and here they let themselves go, but earlier the soul of the song only comes to peeping and longing and being small-voiced. — But with the Italians there is immediately longing-free sound, and the metal of the nature from the first moment on, ignited and in motion; the first sound is freedom and passion, — the first tone immediately goes with free breast and soul blessed into the fray! — the divine Furore is from the start melodic

My dearest Marie,

The air in Vienna is thick with dust and music, but I am well. Tonight, the Kleins kept their word, and we sat closer to the stage than before. The Italian company performed Figaro, and I must confess, the proximity changed everything. I did not merely hear the drama; I felt the tension of the characters’ fates pressing in. Lablache’s Figaro was a whirlwind of wit, while Dardanelli’s Countess held a stillness that was almost painful to watch. The music was not just heard; it was a movement of the spirit, resolving into a freedom that felt tangible. It is a reminder that art, like the state, is the actuality of the ethical idea made visible. We are exhausted but content. The journey is long, but moments like this make the road bearable. I miss your quiet presence at home.

Your devoted,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The evening here in Vienna is quite warm, and the air in the opera house was thick with the scent of perfume and smoke. We sat closer to the stage than before, which made the experience vivid, though perhaps less comfortable for my neck. The Kleins extended their stay just for this, and I confess their enthusiasm was contagious.

Lablache was Figaro; he has a lightness about him that is almost natural, not forced. Fodor as Susanna is exquisite, and Donzelli’s Count had a dignity that felt less like acting and more like memory. Dardanelli’s Countess was lovely, though I found myself thinking of how Mozart’s music holds the soul in tension, moving from the particular complaint to a universal resolution. It is a small mirror of the spirit’s journey.

I am tired but happy. I hope you are well, and that the boys are behaving. I shall write again soon.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The Kleins extended their stay over Sunday, and we attended *The Marriage of Figaro* this evening. I sat nearer the stage than last time, which made the detail of the acting quite vivid. Lablache is a true Figaro; his agility matches the character’s wit perfectly. Fodor as Susanna was charming, and Dardanelli gave the Countess a dignity that made her jealousy palpable. Donzelli’s Count was commanding, though perhaps too stern for the lighter moments.

The music, of course, remains the supreme architecture. Mozart’s harmony resolves all tension into a higher unity, much like the spirit finding its home in the state. It is a delight to see art elevate the soul so effortlessly. I am tired but happy, having enjoyed a fine dinner with the Kleins beforehand. Please give my love to the boys.

Your devoted
G.W.F. Hegel

To bring this to a close, I was in the evening—where?—at Mozart’s *The Marriage of Figaro*. The Kleins stayed on Sunday for that reason. I had to admit to myself that the Italian voices in this more restrained music did not seem to have as much opportunity to develop their brilliant runs, which had been so sweet to hear; but in themselves, with what perfection were the arias, duets, etc., especially the recitatives, delivered—the latter are entirely the artist’s own natural creations. Lablache, what a Figaro! Fodor as Susanna—she would indeed have had to be more beautiful and taller for this role. Signora Dardanelli as the Countess; I sat closer to the stage this time than the first time I saw her—what a beautiful woman, a lovely Italian head, and a calmness, nobility in posture and action—very lovely, beautiful decorum—I almost fell into your situation and would have fallen in love with this woman! She is in fact most charming. Donzelli as the Count—compared rather unfavorably to her; such situations are not good for him.

My dearest Marie,

The air in Vienna is thick with culture, and I am somewhat exhausted by the excess of it. I spent three hours today in the Esterhazy gallery. The Prince, hearing a professor from Berlin had arrived, insisted I see the private cabinet. It is a magnificent collection, though I found myself thinking of how such private hoarding contrasts with the public spirit of a state.

I dined with Professor Sonnleitner and a man from Padua. We spoke of antiquities, but mostly of the wine, which was excellent. In the evening, I attended Rossini’s *Corradino*. The music is dazzling, full of that Italian lightness, though I confess I found the drama somewhat thin. It moves the senses, certainly, but does it move the spirit?

I am tired but content. Think of me by the fire in Berlin.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The heat here is stifling, but the spirit is invigorated. I spent the morning deep in the Esterhazy collection. The Prince, hearing of my presence, had his valet guide me through the private cabinet. It was a magnificent survey of the ethical life’s historical artifacts, though I found the arrangement somewhat arbitrary. I lunched with Sonnleitner and a Paduan professor; good wine, sharp conversation.

Evening brought Rossini’s *Corradino*. The music is a torrent, overwhelming the intellect with pure sensation before reason can settle it. It is effective, certainly, but lacks the dialectical tension of true art. I am tired, yet the journey sharpens my thoughts. Think of me as I walk these imperial streets.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The day was full. I visited the Esterhazy gallery again this morning, from nine until eleven. The Prince, hearing a professor from Berlin was in his city, had a valet show me everything, including the private cabinet. It is impressive, though one sees the taste of a collector rather than the spirit of a state.

I lunched at an inn with Professor Sonnleitner, director of the antiquities cabinet, and a gentleman from Padua. We spoke of antiquities, but mostly of the state of German scholarship. The wine was good, and the company polite, if a bit dull.

In the evening, I went to the opera to hear Rossini’s *Corradino*. The music is a storm of sensation, loud and fast, lacking the deep, quiet structure of the old German masters. It appeals to the ear but leaves the mind unengaged. I am tired now, and the heat in the room is oppressive. I miss the cool of our study in Berlin. Give my love to the boys.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F. Hegel

Now this morning, for the third time, out to the Esterházy Collection; treasures to be admired without end! — one really cannot get enough of them. — The finest pieces are in the Prince’s private room, a garden room in the pavilion — next to the castle, where the great gallery is; the Prince was in this room and, as he heard me walking around, he asked who it was? — since it was not one of the public days; — he was pleased to hear that it was a Berlin professor who had already come for the third time and ordered the valet to show me everything, and as he soon drove off, I was also able to see the magnificent pieces of the cabinet once more — what a living room! — This Prince can travel a few miles from Vienna on his own land and property right up to the Turkish border. — Stayed there from 9 to 11 o’clock, — then — half an hour to go home, — changed clothes — to the Antiquities Cabinet, whose director, Prof. Sonnleitner, had invited me — he is unmarried — to lunch with him at an inn with a professor from Padua — a very learned and amiable man. We scholars are immediately much more at home with one another than with bankers, for example. — Then some walks in the city, — finally also to the Italian Opera and, as I had so much wished, Corradino il cuor di ferro, — which was melted and softened by the charming Dardanelli; — how sweetly she sang — and how David sang again with her! I did not contradict a man with whom I had entered into conversation at dinner last evening, who even went so far as to claim that Rossini’s music is music for the heart.

My dearest Marie,

The long spell of fair weather has finally broken. The air feels different tonight, a bit heavier, as if the city is settling in for a proper autumn. The Kleins departed this morning. Our time together was brief and largely confined to our meals; we did little sightseeing, which I confess I found rather convenient. I prefer the company of good food and conversation to wandering the streets in the heat, though I suspect you would have enjoyed the promenades.

I intend to stay a few more days. There are places I have not yet visited, and now that the oppressive heat has lifted, I feel I can actually walk again without feeling like a boiled egg. I shall take my time, perhaps visit the museum properly, and enjoy a quiet evening with a glass of wine and a good book. Do not worry. I am comfortable, and the change in weather feels like a relief.

Yours affectionately,

G.

My dearest Marie,

The spell of fair weather is broken. The air in Vienna has turned heavy and grey, and with it, the Kleins have departed. We did little more than share meals during their brief stay, but it was pleasant to have company while the sun still shone. I have decided to remain a few more days. There are corners of this city I have not yet walked, and now that the rain has come, I can see them better through the quiet.

I am not in a hurry to return to Berlin. The journey is slow, which suits me. I hope you and the boys are well. Tell Karl to keep his studies steady; do not let him slacken now that I am away. I will write again when I have settled into my next inn.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The fair weather has finally broken in Vienna. The air is heavy, and the city feels quite different under this grey sky. The Kleins left this morning, having spent their stay mostly at our table rather than wandering the sights. I suspect they find the effort of sightseeing too great for their taste, preferring the comfort of a good meal and conversation.

I shall remain a few days longer. I want to see the places I have missed while the crowds are thinner and the light is softer. There is a certain melancholy in the evening here, but it suits my mood. I think of you and the boys in Berlin, wrapped in the familiar warmth of home. I hope Karl and Immanuel are studying well and that Ludwig is behaving himself.

Do not worry about me. I am well, if a bit tired from the travel. I will write again soon.

Your loving
G.W.F.

The fine weather is now past, but the pleasant days in Aranjuez are not quite over, for I shall spend a few more here; there is still much that I do not know. But to consider this, and what I already know, more exhaustively, a few weeks would certainly not have been enough. — This morning the Kleins are leaving from here; although it was hardly possible for us to go about and see things together much, we did see each other at table, and it was a very pleasant company.

My dearest Marie,

The light here in Vienna is peculiar, softening the edges of things. I spent the afternoon at the Belvedere; the paintings do not shout, but they hold a quiet dignity that speaks to the mind without demanding it.

Tonight, however, the mind was overwhelmed by the senses. I attended Rossini’s *Barber of Seville*. The Partheys, as I urged them, were there to share the experience. Lablache’s Figaro is a marvel of wit, and the company’s energy is infectious. The audience’s applause was not merely polite; it was a collective affirmation of the joy on stage, breaking the usual reserve of the Viennese. It reminded me that art, at its height, is the liberation of spirit through form.

I am tired but happy. The journey is long, but such moments make the miles worthwhile. Think of me as I sit here, writing by candlelight, longing for our table in Berlin.

Your loving,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The heat in Vienna is immense, but the evening was a delight. I spent two hours at the Belvedere, then settled into the opera house for Rossini’s *Barber of Seville*. Lablache was a magnificent Figaro, and young de Franco, though new, held his own against Ambrogi’s Bartolo. The audience here is quite unlike Berlin; they clapped after nearly every scene, forcing the singers to return again and again. I read the theatre notices with amusement at their enthusiasm.

I must confess, the Partheys accompanied me, as I urged them to do at every performance. They are charming company, though their constant chatter about the soprano’s hair almost made me miss the finale. I am tired, but my spirits are high. I miss your quiet counsel and the sound of the house in Berlin. Give my love to the boys.

Your devoted
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The Vienna evening was not what one might expect. I spent two hours at the Belvedere, letting the light do its work on the canvases, before surrendering to the opera. Rossini’s *Barber* was a spectacle of noise rather than soul. Lablache’s Figaro is a mere acrobat, and the audience, lacking taste for the whole, clapped wildly at every entrance, demanding encores until the singers returned to their seats. It is all surface, all gesture.

I urged the Partheys to attend, and they were obliging, if not entirely convinced. I read the theatre paper afterward; the critics praise the company’s technical precision, ignoring the lack of deeper spirit. I am weary from the heat and the bustle. I miss the quiet of our rooms in Berlin, and the sound of your voice. Pray tell the boys I am well, though my ears are ringing.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.

In the afternoon I spent a few more hours at the Belvedere and then attended Rossini's Figaro. What a Figaro Lablache is! What a Rosine Mde Fodor is! She is a perfect singer; what beauty, grace, art, freedom, and taste in her singing! And the excellent Lablache, what a bass! And how cheerful and freely comic, with nothing low or vulgar anywhere. When the entire chorus sings together, and the orchestra likewise rushes in fortissimo with all its might, it sounds most certainly as if he were singing solo, and this entirely without strain, without shouting, without a screaming tone. Ambrogi was also very good again as Dr. Bartolo, and then there was a new singer, de Franco. It is a whole hedge, partly of the most excellent, partly of flawless excellence. But what a part we the public take! Three to four actors are applauded each time at their first appearance, then every passage is applauded—or bravo! bravi! is called out, then after each scene they are immoderately applauded, the singer thanks and goes off, but the applauding continues with sustained strength, so that he or she is not merely clapped, but rather clapped out. At the end of the piece, however, no calling out or set phrases take place. So, repeated Party and others, one cannot see the Figaro performed anywhere else in Italy. I read today in a Viennese theater sheet that the most experienced are of one opinion that, according to their longest memory, no such Italian company has been in Vienna for 50 years, and certainly will not come again for the next 50 years. The Party people, after I had argued them into it, naturally did not miss a single performance and were collectively most delighted, even though they disparaged the Rossinian music, which sometimes also makes me bored as music.

My dearest Marie,

The rain here is relentless, turning the streets into rivers, but I could not rest. After lunch, I hired a carriage to Nussdorf despite the weather. The air was thick and heavy, yet I felt a strange lightness. On the road, I saw a large pear tree, its fruit long since harvested, yet it was in full blossom again. It seemed absurd, a defiance of the natural order, but there was a certain stubborn vitality in it. I enclosed two of the blossoms in this letter for you. They are not beautiful, but they are a sign that life persists even when it seems out of place or out of season.

I think of you and the boys often. The journey is wearying, but the mind is active. I hope the news finds you well. I shall write again soon.

Yours,
Georg Wilhelm

My dearest Marie,

The rain here has been unceasing since Sunday, yet I could not resist the damp. I took a carriage to the Augarten and Nussdorf, where the air was thick but the light strange and beautiful.

I write this by candlelight, and I enclose two small pear blossoms. You will find them odd: the tree’s fruit was already gathered, yet here it is in full bloom again. I do not know how to explain it except to say that life refuses to be contained by a single season. It returns, persistent and strange, much like our own thoughts when we are away from home.

I hope Karl and Immanuel are well. I think of you often in this quiet, wet evening. The journey is tiring, but there is a certain pleasure in these solitary observations. I shall rest now, as the rain does not seem inclined to stop.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The rain here has been relentless since Sunday, yet I could not resist the damp. I took a carriage to the Augarten and on to Nussdorf, where the air was thick and heavy. Along the road, I stopped before a large pear tree. Its fruit had already been gathered, yet there, against all reason, it stood in full bloom again.

It struck me with a strange force: the tree, having given its substance, now returns to its first, most delicate state. It is a kind of life that refuses to be exhausted by its own productivity. I have enclosed two of these blossoms in this letter. They are fragile, but they carry the scent of that impossible recurrence.

The journey is tiring, but the mind is clear. I think of you and the boys often. When will I be back to sit by our fireside?

Your loving husband,
G.W.F.

But now it began to rain terribly at night, all through Sunday and still this morning! What is this to become! Yet one must not give up hope. On Sunday morning I was glad that it was raining so hard—I had to rest once— but after dinner I had myself driven to the Augarten and to Nußdorf, despite the weather, on the way to which I saw a pear tree, as large as a pear tree can be, covered with blossoms; it has already borne fruit; I enclose here a little blossom, one for you, the other for those who themselves have blossomed from this land, as a sign of how greatly I recognize and value the excellence of such soil. — How the Augarten and Nußdorf are, I have provisionally gathered from this and found them very beautiful...

My dearest Marie,

The morning was bright, and I spent it in the Imperial Library. I had hoped to see more, but I lingered over the Raphael and the Marcantonios. They are masterpieces, truly. I left a small tip for the attendant; it is the only way to keep the doors open and the eyes off one’s back. I find that in Vienna, as everywhere, a little coin smooths the path.

Yesterday’s ballet was a spectacle, though I confess I found the German dancer Eberle less convincing than the critics did. The weather has finally cleared, and the air feels lighter. I am tired, as one always is after a day of looking at other men’s genius, but my spirits are good. I am thinking of you and the boys constantly. Do not worry about me; I am eating well, and the wine here is not half bad.

I shall write again soon.

Your affectionate,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The weather finally cleared this afternoon, and I took a long walk to clear my head. This morning I spent several hours at the Imperial Library, examining works by Raphael and Marcantonio. I tipped the attendants well, for they were helpful, and the collections are open free on fixed days, a pleasant arrangement.

Last evening, the programme ended with the first act of a ballet featuring the German dancer Eberle. I found the performance adequate, though my mind was already on the drawings. I am thinking of you and the boys here. The city is vibrant, but there is no home like Berlin. I hope Karl and Immanuel are well and that Ludwig is behaving himself.

I shall return to the library tomorrow if the light permits. Please give my love to the household.

Your devoted husband,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The sun broke through the clouds this afternoon, and I walked the streets with a lightness I had not felt since we left Berlin. This morning I visited the Imperial Library. The attendants were courteous, and I ensured they were well rewarded for their time; it is a small kindness that keeps the spirit of the place pleasant. I stood before Raphael’s works, contemplating how the divine manifests through the human form, and Marcantonio’s engravings, which capture that same ideal with such precision.

Last evening’s ballet was a spectacle of the senses, particularly the performance of the German dancer Eberle. It reminded me how art, even in its lighter forms, participates in the universal by elevating the particular to the ideal. I miss your company in these quiet moments of reflection. The journey is tiring but instructive.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

Current and blessed, it penetrates and liberates every situation! Ask the Milder whether it is not so; — she herself, in happy; not Rossini’s music, is this, for her tone, sound, and action are from the house and from the beginning out of passion and soulful penetration, — You yourself also feel this, when in re-echoes or even only in memory this fullness re-echoes in you, lives on, and storms on. — It would still be worth mentioning that finally the first act of yesterday’s ballet was performed; Eberle, a German, danced excellently, though not quite the Italian manner of a Torelli, who with her admirable manners and even more her Roman physiognomy, gave me also an idea of Italian dancing. — But now from these profane observations and plays of the 5th Oct.... The weather has cleared up again this afternoon; certainly the Berliner Dittmar has predicted this, — for here first and in the local newspapers I see how much this prophet here, — where his fatherland is not, — counts; for which reason I also did not stay in Swabia, but went over Nuremberg to Berlin. To return to my dry historical relation, — this morning early to the Imperial and Royal Library, having been with Raphael and Marc Anton. What soulful delicacy, what Unica! Along with this also again a prosaic remark: — here one sees on certain days (in the Imperial and Royal Library every day) all the treasures of artistic genius — free of charge; to the serving attendants one gives perhaps a tip and I have always, even when it was not necessary, given tips, to do honor at least to the royal Prussian professorship. On the other hand, the Berlin-Potsdam dirtiness is notorious here and in the whole world! — and I, royal Professor publ. ordin. at the royal university in Berlin (and indeed Professor of the subject, namely of Philosophy, as the

My dearest Marie,

The heat here in Prague is oppressive, a thick blanket that seems to press down upon the spirit. I spent this afternoon wandering the churches and galleries, seeking some coolness among the old paintings, yet the air remains heavy. It is a strange sensation, to be so far from our quiet Berlin evenings, walking alone through these crowded streets.

I had the pleasure of lunching with my host’s family today. They are a cheerful lot, and after the meal, we drove out to a pleasure ground on the outskirts. The carriage ride was dusty, but the fresh air did me good. I dine with them again tomorrow, so do not worry for my sustenance, only for my patience. I miss your company and the comfort of our home. The journey is long, but I am making my way.

Yours,
Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The heat in Prague is becoming quite oppressive, but I have made the most of it. This morning I wandered through the galleries and churches, my eyes tired but my mind content. Yesterday we spent four hours at Karlstein; the old paintings there possess a dignity that modern works lack, a quietude that suits the spirit.

We are staying with my uncle’s family. They are charming, and this afternoon they drove us in a carriage to a pleasure ground outside the town. The air there is fresher, and I enjoyed the walk immensely. It is a relief to escape the dust of the city streets for a few hours. I dine with them again tomorrow, which will give me a proper break from my own lodgings.

I think of you and the boys often. The journey is tiring, but the company is good. I shall write again from Vienna.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The heat in Prague is oppressive today, but I found relief in the coolness of the old churches and galleries. I spent the morning revisiting the galleries, finding a certain quiet dignity in the old masters that contrasts sharply with the bustle of the city. At midday, I lunched with my host’s family. They are charming, though the conversation drifted from politics to the absurdity of the local theater.

In the afternoon, we took the carriage to the pleasure ground outside the town. The air was fresher there, and I watched the families strolling with a detached amusement. It is a spectacle of modern leisure, yet one cannot help but see the underlying structure of social habit in every smile and gesture. I shall dine with them again tomorrow before I continue my journey.

Do not worry for me. I am well, if somewhat tired by the sun. I think of you and the boys constantly.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F.

Friday, September 17. Yesterday I spent the whole day on a trip to Carlstein, an old castle four hours from here, where old paintings still hang, but otherwise there is nothing to see; — this morning I visited the churches and galleries, partly repeating what I had seen before, and have finished my business, i.e., seeing the sights. Yesterday’s tour with its heat, as well as the heat this morning, had made me very weak and affected me; — lunch at Uncle’s house today restored me wonderfully. After the meal, Mr. O. took us by carriage to a very pleasant place of amusement — here all the foliage is still firm and green, although it has not rained for a long time. Tomorrow I shall dine with the same family again; I am very well with them and with their heartfelt, friendly reception...

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Metz this afternoon, the light already softening on the Moselle. I walked the ramparts to catch the valley below, a stillness that suits the end of a day’s labor. The cathedral looms from outside, imposing but distant; I have no time to enter its mysteries tonight, only to observe its stone.

Dinner was decent, though I found the company at the theatre rather tedious. It was crowded with garrison officers, their laughter loud and their attention short. They watched a vaudeville with a distraction that reminded me of students who have not yet learned the discipline of the mind. One learns little from such spectacle, but I confess the wine was better than the play.

I have secured a seat in the front coupé for our departure to Paris tomorrow. The journey will be long, and the heat oppressive, but I look forward to the movement. Do not worry for me; I am well enough to endure the dust and the noise.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I write from Metz, the evening air cool after a long day. The town is quiet, save for the garrison officers who crowded the theatre tonight. I watched a vaudeville and a play, but my mind wandered to the view from the ramparts. The Moselle winds through the valley, a ribbon of silver in the twilight. It is a beautiful sight, reminding me of the Rhine, yet distinct in its character.

I have secured a front coupé for the diligence to Paris tomorrow. The journey should be swift. I walked the streets before dinner, noting the architecture and the life within. It is good to be moving again, to see the world unfold before me. The cathedral looms large, a testament to centuries of faith and stone.

I think of you and the boys in Berlin. The distance feels less when one is traveling with purpose. Pray for a smooth crossing of the frontier.

Your loving,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Metz this afternoon and have secured a front seat in the coupé for tomorrow’s diligence to Paris. The heat was oppressive, but I managed a walk along the ramparts before dinner. The view of the Moselle valley was quite magnificent, though the cathedral, seen only from the outside, lacks the interior grandeur one might expect. It is a sturdy building, certainly, but I confess I found the exterior somewhat austere.

After the meal, I attended the theatre. The house was full of garrison officers, their uniforms glittering under the chandeliers. We saw a play followed by a vaudeville. The acting was competent, if not inspiring, and the music was pleasant enough to pass the time. I found the atmosphere light and sociable, a welcome change from the quiet of Berlin. I am tired but content. Please give my regards to the boys. I hope to reach Paris by evening.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

At this moment, after 3 p.m., I arrive here; I could immediately depart for Paris at 5 o'clock; but according to my usual system, I intend to rest again. So I am, in fact, in France! Evening. I have already had myself registered in the Lafitte diligence in the Coupé; that is the front compartment of the carriage; there are three boxes one behind the other; the middle one is called l'interieur and the rear one Cabriolet; the Coupé has 3 seats side by side, facing forward, and is closed with windows, not open, like the so-called Cabriolets on our express post coaches. Before dinner I briefly viewed the city somewhat, the cathedral from the outside and especially the view from a part of the rampart, which is most charming; the valley, through which the Moselle flows, bounded by gentle hills, wider, richer in buildings and villages, and more attractive than the surroundings of Dresden. Since Metz is a significant fortress, the garrison is numerous. After dinner I went to the theater, which was full of officers; hardly a dozen women and civilians; List against List, — also in Germany on the theater, — and then a Vaudeville, all nonsensical — and very cold — stuff, but played and spoken with such liveliness that I understood hardly a word, especially from the wretched singing.

My dearest Marie,

Paris keeps its promise. We drove to the abattoir today; the machinery of death here is as organized as life, a stark reminder of necessity. We also visited the Bourse, where money dances, and Montmartre, from which the city stretches out like a vast, breathing body. The Palace of the Deputies stands firm, a symbol of the ethical state actualized in law.

Dinner was lively with Cousin and Fauriel. Fauriel’s Greek folk songs are charming, though he speaks of them as curiosities rather than the soul of a people. I have also enjoyed Mignet and Thiers; their history is sharp, though perhaps too much concerned with events and not enough with spirit.

I think of you and the boys constantly. The air is thick with history, but my heart remains in Berlin. Write soon.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

Paris is a spectacle of contradiction. Today we visited the abattoir, a grim reminder of the material basis of life, and then the Bourse, where the spirit of capital dances to a different tune. From Montmartre, one sees the whole city laid out like a logical proposition, every street a term in the argument of human freedom. I dined with Cousin and Fauriel. Fauriel, the editor of Greek folk songs, is a charming man; there is something in their ancient melodies that speaks to the soul, though I confess the political chatter of the Chamber of Deputies left me cold. It is all very lively, but I find myself missing the quiet order of our home and the sharp clarity of our conversations. The air here is thick with history, but I long for the peace of Berlin. Do not worry; I am well, if perhaps a bit tired.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The light here is fading, and I find myself reflecting on the day’s strange juxtapositions. We visited the abattoir, that place of necessary violence, and then the Bourse, where the life of the city pulses in pure abstraction. It is a vivid reminder that the ethical life of the state is not a static ideal, but a living process where spirit externalizes itself into law and economy.

I dined with Cousin and Fauriel. We spoke of Greek folk songs, and I was struck by how the particularity of a people’s history must first be preserved in its art before it can be elevated into universal consciousness. It is a gentle counterpoint to the rigid formalism we often encounter.

My thoughts are with you and the boys. The journey is tiring, but the spirit of the place is stimulating. I hope Karl and Immanuel are well and that Ludwig is settling into his studies.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

You notice that I do not write about Paris with such fire and enthusiasm as I did from Vienna, and that you have communicated much to the friends; that may be so, but everything I write is too fleeting to be capable of much communication. You must take into account that my ill health has caused me to lose much time, and then that everything is so enormously vast and sprawling that one must be externally quite vigorous to encompass more, and must stay here longer to come into deeper contacts and penetrations. It is a most interesting ground, but a few weeks are only enough to get out of the stupor and into the habit of all the brilliant and manifold things. Today, for example, we drove to an abattoir, i.e., a slaughterhouse—in which city in the world would I drive to a slaughterhouse?—but this is one of the curiosities that Paris owes to Napoleon, as it does to a hundred other great things. Then we were on the Montmartre, where one overlooks the wealth of houses in Paris and the splendid, fertile, lively surroundings; also in the Palace of the Chamber of Deputies. We saw the Stock Exchange, still laid out by Napoleon, beforehand, what a temple! At half past six o’clock I dined with Cousin and Fauriel (the editor of the Greek songs, which have also been translated into German). A few days ago we dined together with Mignet, Thiers, Mustoxidis, Fauriel, and so on; in short, one must be in Paris for half a year to become more familiar with everything for which one takes a deeper interest, and, as said, through habit to lose all interest in what is striking and worth seeing for the first period. Cousin has often laughed at me when I saw and found remarkable what the conscience of a traveler and the Manual of the Foreigner prescribed to see.

My dearest Marie,

I hope the children are well and that Karl is not too absorbed in his studies tonight. I write from Paris, where the air is thick with September damp.

Yesterday I took a carriage to Saint-Cloud. The Seine was grey and sluggish, but the view from the terrace was grand enough to remind me that nature, however beautiful, lacks the inner movement of Spirit.

Tonight, however, I sat through a three-act ballet on a sleepwalker. It was absurd. The hero is found in a nobleman’s bed, then mimes crossing a roof with a lantern. Only the first act was actually danced; the rest was mere pantomime. The audience laughed, but I felt only a profound irritation. To see human freedom reduced to such mechanical, dream-like posturing is painful. It is a spirit asleep, yet it does not even have the dignity of true slumber.

I miss our walks in the Tiergarten. Pray send my regards to Ludwig.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I write from Paris, exhausted but delighted. Yesterday I walked at Saint-Cloud, watching the Seine flow by; the water was calm, reflecting the autumn light in a way that reminded me of the quiet dignity of the Rhine. But tonight was peculiar. I attended a three-act ballet concerning a sleepwalker found in a nobleman’s bedroom, later seen crossing a roof with a lantern. It was strange: only the first act was danced; the rest was merely mimed. One sees the tension between movement and stillness, the body acting without the full presence of the soul. It is a strange spectacle, yet it captures something of the unconscious mind’s wanderings.

I am safe and well, though the French air is thick. I think of you and the boys in Berlin. The journey continues, but my heart remains with you.

Your loving,
Wilhelm

My dearest Marie,

The day has been a strange succession of images. Yesterday at Saint-Cloud, the Seine moved with a quiet dignity, a reminder that nature does not rush to its own end. But tonight, I sat in the theatre for a ballet that defied all logic. The subject was a sleepwalker found in a nobleman’s bed, later seen crossing a roof with a lantern. It was a spectacle of pure appearance, where the body moves without the will’s direction. The first act was danced; the rest was merely mimed. It struck me as a perfect allegory of the undetermined spirit, drifting through the ethical sphere without conscious intent.

I am tired, but my mind is active. The absurdity of the performance, the stillness of the river, the heat of the evening—they all press against each other. I hope Karl and Immanuel are well. I miss your steady presence here in Berlin.

Your loving,
G.W.F.

What is there to say about the ballet? — a subject that no one has yet thought to treat in a ballet, and which would hardly occur to anyone else — namely, a sleepwalker. In the first act, there is dancing — with all its complications; yet there is a plot. Grace, cheerfulness, agility (the corps de ballet has it too!); in the second act, a sleepwalker appears, coming through the window on a ladder with a lantern in her hand, into the master of the house’s bedroom, lies down — after having knelt and prayed (the French around me said she was a Protestant, since it is not a church in which she prays; Protestant churches are officially called temples here). — The master — out of reverence — climbs out of the same window and leaves her alone — great applause for this virtuous behavior. The third act begins with the greatest anger of the sleepwalker’s fiancé, that she was found sleeping in a gentleman’s room. The gentleman explains to him and to the entire audience that she came into his room as a sleepwalker; they do not want to comprehend or understand it; then she appears once more on the roof, strolling with the lantern and marching down from a high, dangerously collapsed wall; — reconciliation ends everything. — In the last two acts, there is no more dancing — but much grace and liveliness in the pantomime, which admittedly cannot be understandable everywhere. — Yesterday I was in St. Cloud — beautiful surroundings — on the bank of the Seine, whose curves here form almost a complete circle, enclosing the vineyard hill; before one lies Paris with its beautiful towers and domes and countless houses. —

My dearest Marie,

The air here is sharp, and the light on the Seine tonight is unlike anything we have seen in Berlin. I have been to Saint-Denis and Montmorency. The cathedral at Saint-Denis is draped in black for a recent funeral; it is a heavy, solemn sight, reminding one that even kings are subject to the march of history. From Montmorency, I rode a donkey to Rousseau’s Hermitage. It is a modest place, but the view from the heights above the town is commanding. I could see all of Paris, with Montmartre rising in the distance. It struck me how the capital looks from here—not as a city of noise, but as a vast, living organism of the spirit. The journey has been tiring, but the mind is refreshed. I miss your presence and the comfort of our home. Do not worry about me; I am well, if a little dusty. Write soon.

Your loving
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The day was warm and pleasant. We drove to Saint-Denis, where the cathedral still wore black for a recent funeral—a stark reminder of mortality even in the heart of France. From there to Montmorency, where I took a donkey to Rousseau’s Hermitage. The little beast was stubborn, but the climb to the heights was worth the effort. Looking back, one sees Paris stretching out, with Montmartre rising in the distance. It is a strange perspective to view the capital from such a rural vantage point. I confess I enjoyed the physical exertion more than the philosophical associations. The air is clear, and the light is fading beautifully over the Seine. I hope your health remains good in Berlin. I shall dine well tonight and sleep soundly.

Your loving,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

The drive to Saint-Denis and Montmorency was pleasant, though the cathedral’s black drapery for a funeral gave the morning a solemn air. I rode a donkey to the Hermitage, Rousseau’s old retreat, and we climbed the heights. From there, the view of Paris and Montmartre was magnificent. It is strange to see the city from such a distance, reduced to a patchwork of roofs and smoke.

I thought of how we often chase grandeur in the public square, when the true perspective comes only from a quiet elevation. The day was warm, and the air fresh. I feel rested, though my legs ache from the climb. Please tell the boys that Father is well and has seen the very spot where the *Social Contract* was born, if only in the ruins of a garden.

I miss you and the comfort of our Berlin home. Write soon.

Your loving,
G.W.F. Hegel

I wrote the above yesterday morning — at 10 o’clock I drove with Raumer and his company to St. Denis and Montmoreney. There is the famous cathedral, the burial place of the Kings of France, — it was still hung with black inside from a funeral service the previous day — in Montmoreney there is an estate, called the Hermitage, where Rousseau lived for a time?), and therefore — there are many small relics (there), also a rose bush that he planted — it is frequently visited in a pilgrim-like manner and on donkeys — (also by me with such eagerness) — . Montmoreney lies high and one ascends the higher heights behind it, — one has Paris at a distance of two hours, Montmartre and the large, rich plain dotted with villages and country houses before one. — It is beautiful around Paris, fertile, varied, — no wonder that so much life is lived in the country. This evening I am going to the Italian Opera to hear the Pesaroni — highly praised — in the morning still to the Gallery in the Louvre.

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Brussels this evening, exhausted but in good spirits. I am staying at the house of my friend Van Ghert, whose hospitality is most welcome. Madame Van Ghert was kind enough to cut a fresh quill for me, a small gesture that made the room feel less like an inn and more like home.

I have received your letter from the post office, which I have read with great pleasure. It is a comfort to hear of the household’s peace while I am away. The journey has been steady, though the fatigue accumulates. I find myself thinking of our sons and the quiet order of our Berlin home more than usual.

I shall not stay long. The road calls, and I must continue my observations of this part of the world. I hope this letter finds you well and that the boys are behaving as they should.

Your loving Georg

My dearest Marie,

I write to you from the house of my friend van Ghert in Brussels. The evening is quiet, and I have taken a moment to rest my eyes after the journey. Madame van Ghert was kind enough to cut a quill pen for me this afternoon; it is sharp and cuts the paper well, which is all a man can ask for in these days. I also retrieved your letter from the post office earlier. Your words were a great comfort to me on the road.

I think of you and the boys often. The air here is cool, and I find myself longing for the warmth of our home in Berlin. I hope your health is good and that Karl and Immanuel are diligent in their studies. I shall continue my journey soon, but for tonight, I am content to sit by the fire and write to you.

Yours always,

G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

I have reached Brussels safely and am staying with van Ghert. The house is comfortable, and Madame van Ghert, a kind soul, insisted on cutting my quill pen herself. It is a small gesture, but it reminds me that one finds hospitality not only in grand salons but in the quiet domesticity of good friends.

I fetched our letter from the post office. It is a relief to hold your handwriting after the dust of the road. The journey is wearying, yet the change of air is good. I think of you and the boys often, especially as I sit in this quiet room. Please do not worry about my health; I am merely tired. I look forward to returning to Berlin, where the air is cleaner and the cards sharper.

Give my love to Karl and Immanuel.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.

Also Brussels! in the house of my friend Mr. van Ghert)) and with a quill that Mde van Ghert has just cut for me, and indeed in a trice, with a single press. — You see hereby that it has become serious, to renounce Paris, — which you, in your letter, which I have just had fetched from the post, — wanted to doubt would happen so soon...

My dearest Marie,

The heat was stifling, but the journey to Bruges has been agreeable enough. I arrived at eight after boarding a canal barge at two. The cabin was pleasantly crowded; passengers read the newspapers or played whist with a fervor that reminded me of our own parlour games. I confess I watched the cards with interest, though I did not join in.

Earlier, in Ghent, I viewed the fragments of the van Eyck altarpiece. The detail is astonishing, a testament to a different kind of spirit. But I find myself thinking less of art and more of the slow, inevitable movement of the state. These canals, these barges, they are not just transport; they are the veins of a commercial order that grows, not as a product of arbitrary will, but as the actuality of the ethical idea.

The air in Bruges is cooler. I hope this letter finds you and the boys well in Berlin. I miss your company and the quiet of our home.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The journey from Brussels to Bruges was a study in contrasts. I left Cousin in Brussels on Friday, viewing the Ghent Altarpiece fragments before boarding a canal barge. It was a strange vessel: while the water lapped against the hull, the cabin filled with the sharp clatter of whist and the rustle of newspapers. I found myself observing how men seek distraction in the small, even as the river carries them toward the great.

We arrived in Bruges at eight, the evening air cool and damp. I am resting now, tired but content. The landscape here is flat, yet the history feels heavy, almost suffocating in its density. I think of our home, of the quiet order we have built, and how different it is from this transient, noisy passage. I hope you and the boys are well. I miss your company and the silence of our study.

Yours ever,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

I am writing from Bruges, having arrived this evening after a day of varied travel. I left Brussels on Friday, pausing in Ghent to examine the fragments of the van Eyck altarpiece. The color remains startlingly alive, even after centuries; it is a testament to how art preserves the spirit of its age, distinct from the dry chronicles of history.

The journey to Bruges was by canal barge. The cabin was crowded, and as is the custom, several gentlemen played whist with considerable intensity while others read. I found the motion of the water soothing, a gentle rhythm that contrasts sharply with the jolting of the diligence. The air here is cool, and the evening light on the canal is quite beautiful. I think of you and the boys in Berlin, and the comfort of our home. I shall continue onward to France tomorrow, but for now, I rest.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.

On Friday morning I set out — my cousin remained in Brussels — on the diligence to Ghent, saw what could be seen of the Eyck painting there (of which we have the fine pieces in Berlin), and at 2 o’clock boarded the barge to Bruges on the canal (— it is drawn by horses; in the cabin one reads, plays whist, and so on); at 8 o’clock in the evening I arrived. Ghent has 70,000 inhabitants, Bruges 33,000 — in the exterior of the latter, the peculiar Dutch style of building is entirely preserved, which is already blurred and modernized in Ghent, and even more so in Brussels.

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Koblenz yesterday, though the journey from Kassel was tedious enough. I dined with the Beers, then took a coach to Marburg, where I called briefly on Suabedissen. The heat was oppressive, and I was glad to spend the afternoon in Wetzlar with Schulz’s family. His kindness in showing me the town this morning, and seeing me onto the 10 a.m. mail coach, was a welcome respite from the dust and noise of travel.

I have taken a bath, which has done me good. The Rhine here is grand, but I confess the landscape does not stir the spirit quite as the city does. I miss the quiet of our home and the presence of the boys. I hope this letter finds you and the children well. Do not worry too much about my pace; I am taking things as they come.

Your affectionate,
Georg

My dearest Marie,

I write from Koblenz, where the air is thick with the heat of the Rhine. I have just taken a bath to wash away the dust of the road; it is the first relief I have felt since leaving Kassel. The journey to Marburg was brief but necessary, and I was glad to see Suabedissen, though we had little time. In Wetzlar, however, I found true rest. Schulz’s family received me with such warmth that I spent the whole afternoon and evening among them. This morning he walked me through the town, showing me its quiet corners, before seeing me onto the mail coach.

I think of you and the boys constantly. Berlin feels far away, yet my heart remains there. I hope the heat has not been too oppressive for you. I shall continue on, but for now, I am content to sit here by the river, snuff in hand, and rest my mind.

Your loving,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Koblenz safely, though the journey from Kassel was a long one. I spent a pleasant afternoon with the Schulz family in Wetzlar; they are a good, quiet sort, and I enjoyed their company before catching the mail coach at ten. The heat has been oppressive, but I took a bath this morning which did wonders for my spirits.

I miss our home, the library, and the sound of the boys’ voices. I have been thinking of you constantly. The Rhine here is magnificent, but it lacks the warmth of our hearth. I shall continue on to the next stage tomorrow, but I hope to be back in Berlin before the autumn sets in. Give my love to Karl, Immanuel, and Ludwig.

Your affectionate,
Georg

I have just come from the bath and am writing to you hastily, as the post leaves at 3 o'clock and lunch is approaching. — You can see from the date and the bath taken that I have already advanced about 80 miles and am taking my cure very seriously. — I have first to give you the further report of my journey, which is rather simple. Mr. and Mde Beer will have already told you, before receiving this letter, about the pleasant day we spent together in Cassel, despite the bad weather... The express post only left Cassel on Tuesday evening, so I traveled with a hired coach on Monday the 21st from Cassel to Marburg — without any noteworthy incident; in the evening I was still able to visit Hofrath Suabedissen, Professor of Philosophy, in that bumpy little nest, but he had a whole hedge of female relatives with him, so that I set off again immediately. On Tuesday I drove to Wetzlar, where I first visited Schulz, who lives outside the city in the garden, after dinner; he and his wife had a heartfelt joy over my visit; they are all very healthy and looking well — the children, my godchildren, who were almost sickly, are all very strong and well; the garden is on a hill, and has some buildings lying about 30 steps up the slope; I had to stay with him in the afternoon and evening until 10 o'clock. In the morning Schulz came to me, showed me around the little that was worth seeing, and stayed with me until I boarded the express post at 10 o'clock. — He is with body and soul engaged in very interesting studies; his conversation was very instructive to me; the whole family lives quite happily... Yesterday I arrived in Koblenz at 10 o'clock; the express post from there to Trier leaves already tomorrow; that was too early; I will therefore only depart with it on Monday, — to Trier in one day. Had I been able to calculate it, I could have asked you to write to me in Trier, where I — and that on my birthday — could have received a letter from you; I will drink to your well-being and happiness on that occasion. — Now a heartfelt kiss and greeting, likewise to the boys. In Paris I no longer understand German. — Write to me a lot from Berlin — about you and other things... Greet the friends, Privy Councillor Schulze in particular.

My dearest Marie,

The Louvre closed its doors to us today, the last night before the living artists take over. It was strange, walking through that silence with Raumer and Panofka, knowing the walls belong to history now, not just the present. I saw Alzire and L’École des maris earlier; Mlle Mars is still magnificent, though time has added a weight to her voice that suits the tragedy.

I find myself thinking of our sons. I hope they are not merely playing at freedom, but learning the discipline that makes judgment possible. A child who is not taught to obey will never know the true dignity of doing what is right. I miss our evenings, the cards, the quiet. The air here is thick with expectation, but I am tired.

Tell the boys their father is well, and that he loves them.

Yours,
G.W.F.

My dearest Marie,

The heat here is stifling, yet the mind finds its cool in the Louvre. I returned today to the gallery before the living painters take over the walls. Raumer and Panofka were there; we discussed the transition from ideal to actuality in art, though they lacked the depth to grasp the necessity of the movement. Cousin’s company earlier was pleasant enough, if somewhat superficial.

In the evening, the Théâtre-Français offered a respite. Mlle Mars in *Alzire* possesses a dignity that borders on the tragic, while Leverd in *Emilia* showed the lighter, more immediate side of feeling. It is good to see the ethical life played out on stage, even if the French conception of freedom remains bound to the particular.

I am tired but content. The journey continues, but my thoughts remain with you and the boys in Berlin. Do not worry; I am eating well and keeping my spirits high.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

My dearest Marie,

The light in the Louvre galleries is fading as the exhibition of living painters prepares to take over. I walked the halls again today, thinking of our conversation with Cousin. The art here is vibrant, yet it lacks the profound ethical depth I seek in the historical development of spirit. Raumer and Panofka joined me; their company was pleasant, though I find myself missing the familiar quiet of our study in Berlin.

In the evening, I attended the Théâtre-Français. *Alzire* and *Emilia* were performed with Mlle Mars and Mlle Leverd. The acting was competent, but the dialogue felt thin compared to the weight of true philosophical inquiry. I am tired, yet my mind remains restless. I hope this letter reaches you safely. Tell the boys I am well and think of them often. The journey continues, but my heart remains with you.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

The painting gallery is in the Louvre, — a straight, long hall, vaulted at the top — both sides hung with paintings; — a passage, almost endless, a quarter of an hour long; I had gone through it quickly with Cousin a few days ago, yesterday I wanted to begin the more thorough studies or views, when it turned out that exactly yesterday and today there is still time, — from tomorrow the museum (i.e. the collection of paintings and also the antiquities) is closed for preparation for the painting exhibition of current masters; — there is a great wealth and famous pieces by the noblest masters, which one has seen a hundred times in engravings, present; — by Raphael, Correggio, Leon. da Vinci, Titian and so on, — I am going back again in half an hour, to find Raumer!) and Panofka, whom I met there yesterday, and to make an appointment with them for this afternoon, it is Sunday and church fair in St. Cloud (i.e. fishing in Stralau)?) ; Cousin advises against going; instead there is horse racing at the Champ de Mars. — Raumer has an audience with Mlle Mars today at noon; he must be with all the actresses); Cousin finds it ridiculous to go to her, — to Talma or Mde Pasta, — if they were still here — he would have taken me. By the way Mlle Mars; in the theater I have of course also already been — in the French one twice, — once Alzire by Voltaire and l'école des maris by Moliere — so from the most famous pieces, — the other time in Emilia, tragedy after W. Scott, — an Emilia has Mlle Mars, — then Mlle Leverd (Queen Elizabeth) played, — especially the Mars very charming and noble, of course with peculiarity; one understands Mlle Mars and Leverd every word 7); they play, as the men in general also, much more restrained, with much less pathetic raging than our actors and actresses, — the men are mediocre, Lafond the most famous after Talma, almost like a butcher; — the French are generally calmer and more definite in expressing their feelings than we are, especially you; how often do I say to you, you should say and treat the matter without feeling, yet your liveliness often suits you quite nicely!
